title: A primitive screenshot is one History node, one body and one status line: read the node, the scale bar and the mesh counts
summary: Each figure is a GeoStudio window with a single signed-distance primitive in the History panel, the meshed body in a 3D view, and a status line giving vertex and face counts. It shows that the primitive was built and meshed; the counts let you test, with one identity, whether the surface is closed.

media.alt: GeoStudio window. The History panel lists one node, target: sdf_torus. The 3D view shows a dark torus lying flat on a labelled ground grid, scale bar 1 mm. The status line reads MESH 5848 verts, 11696 faces.

source.caption: GeoStudio screenshot (sandbox run): sdf torus
source.note: Group of 13 GeoStudio screenshots of single signed-distance primitives (7 sandbox runs, 6 toolbar runs). The screenshots are of the owner's own tool. Whether the Resolution box (32) is samples per axis is not stated on the figure.

read_the_figure.question: Did this primitive build into a closed solid of the expected shape and size?
read_the_figure.axes: There are no data axes. The large panel is a 3D perspective view: the ground grid carries numbered tick labels in model units (for the torus they run from about -9 to 5), and the bar at bottom left is a length scale (1 mm for the torus). The left panel is the History: one row per node.
look_at: History panel, left. A primitive figure has exactly one row (for example target: sdf_torus). That row, not the picture, names what was built.
The body in the viewport. Compare its outline with the standard shape: a ring for the torus, a stadium-shaped bar for the capsule and the stroke, a ball for the sphere, a block for the box.
The scale bar. The same bar can read 200 micrometres, 500 micrometres or 1 mm in different screenshots, so two bodies that look equal in size are not necessarily equal.
The MESH line under the viewport: number of vertices (V) and triangles (F). Use it with the identity in the steps below to check that the surface is closed.
The Resolution box (32) and the Rebuild button: the mesh is a sampled approximation of the exact surface, rebuilt on demand.

Toolbar-run versions of the same primitives were produced by clicking the palette instead of the sandbox script. One I opened from the neighbouring features group lists all sixteen nodes in its History and adds a verification block, so check the History panel first.
read_the_figure.proves: That the primitive node was created, evaluated and meshed at the stated resolution into a body whose triangle counts are consistent with one closed surface. It does not prove the dimensions: no parameter values are printed in the window.
if_wrong: The body looks like the right shape but the History row names another primitive: the screenshot was taken at the wrong step.
2V minus F is not 4 for a ball-like body or 0 for a ring-like body: the mesh has boundary edges, duplicate vertices or extra pieces.
The viewport is cropped or the body touches its edge: part of the surface may be outside the view, so the outline is incomplete.
Two screenshots with the same mesh counts but different History rows: the viewport may not have refreshed.
must_check: A length scale is visible and its unit is stated (here micrometres or millimetres).
Dimensions are printed or at least recoverable from the node. They are not printed in these windows, so quantities such as radii are not known from the figure.
The mesh counts are shown and satisfy the closed-surface identity.
The camera angle is stated (the compass at top right and the yaw and pitch label), so shapes are not misjudged from a skewed view.
The exact surface and the sampled mesh are not confused: a coarse mesh can understate curvature.
as_drawn: Values read from the status line of the screenshots I opened. They are exact digits from the window, not estimates.
sdf_torus: 5848 vertices, 11696 faces, scale bar 1 mm. 2V minus F is 0, as for one closed ring-shaped surface.
sdf_capsule: 4320 vertices, 8636 faces, scale bar 500 micrometres. 2V minus F is 4, as for one closed ball-like surface.
sdf_stroke: 4304 vertices, 8604 faces, scale bar 200 micrometres. 2V minus F is 4, again one closed ball-like surface.
I did not open the sphere, box, cone and cylinder screenshots at full size; they follow the same layout.

terms.meaning: A function d(p) giving the distance from point p to the surface, negative inside the body and positive outside. The surface is where d is zero.
A body defined by a short closed formula for d: sphere, box, cylinder, cone, torus, capsule. Larger shapes are built from them.
The set where d equals a constant. The zero level set is the surface of the body.
A surface approximated by triangles: V vertices and F faces. It is what is drawn and what a solver would read.
A mesh in which every edge is shared by exactly two triangles, so it has no boundary and encloses a volume.
A number computed from a mesh, V minus E plus F. It is 2 for a ball-like closed surface, 0 for a torus, and adds up over separate pieces.
All points within distance r of a line segment: a cylinder with hemispherical ends. A stroke is a thick line drawn the same way.
The surface of a ring: a circle of radius r swept around an axis at distance R.

remember: A signed distance is negative inside, zero on the surface and positive outside.
Each primitive is a one-line formula; the screenshot only shows its sampled mesh.
For a closed triangle mesh, F = 2V - 2 chi. A ball-like surface has chi = 2, a torus has chi = 0.
The History panel names the node and the scale bar gives the unit; neither is in the picture of the body.
No dimensions are printed in these windows, so never quote a radius from them.

understand.title: Why a formula can replace a CAD model
understand.text: An SDF primitive is a function you can evaluate at any point. Inside tests, offsets and combinations reduce to arithmetic on the number d. The price is that a surface must be extracted by sampling when you want to draw or mesh it.

understand.title: What the status line is for
understand.text: V and F are free to read and carry topological information. They cannot tell you the size of the body, but they can tell you whether it is one closed piece.

steps.title: A body is the set where the signed distance is not positive
steps.tex: \Omega=\{p:\ d(p)\le 0\},\qquad \partial\Omega=\{p:\ d(p)=0\},\qquad \lVert\nabla d\rVert=1\ \text{(for an exact distance)}
steps.note: The body, its surface and the unit-gradient property. Many tools use functions that are only bounds on the distance; the sign is still right.

steps.title: Sphere
steps.note: Distance to the centre minus the radius. The simplest primitive.

steps.title: Box with half-sizes b
steps.note: The absolute value and the maximum with zero act componentwise. The first term is the distance outside, the second is the negative depth inside.

steps.title: Torus with major radius R and minor radius r
steps.note: The inner square root is the distance from the axis. The outer one is the distance from the core circle. Subtract r for the tube.

steps.title: Capsule between two end points a and b
steps.note: h is the closest point on the segment, kept between the ends by clamping. Distance to that point minus the radius.

steps.title: A closed triangle mesh obeys a counting identity
steps.note: Each triangle has three edges and each edge is shared by two triangles. Eliminating E gives F in terms of V and chi. This is the check applied to the mesh line.

steps.title: Reading the counts
steps.note: Both match one closed surface of the expected type: ring-like and ball-like. Arithmetic checked by computation.

steps.title: Volume of a ring by revolving its disc
steps.note: Pappus's theorem: area A of the profile times the distance its centroid travels. The live revolve scene uses R = 3, r = 1 and gets 6 pi squared.

worked.title: Is a point inside an illustrative torus?
worked.problem: The window does not print the torus dimensions, so take illustrative values R = 1.5 and r = 0.5. Is the point (2.2, 0, 0) inside, on, or outside the surface, and what is the torus volume?

solution.text: Distance from the axis is 2.2. Distance from the core circle is 2.2 minus 1.5.

worked.answer: d = 0.2 > 0, so the point is outside, 0.2 from the surface. The volume is about 7.40 cubic units. Both numbers belong to the illustrative torus, not to the figure.

analyze.q: The capsule and the stroke have almost the same vertex count but different scale bars. What does that say about the mesh, and what does it not say about their sizes?
analyze.hint: The mesh size depends on the sampling resolution, not on the size of the body.

analyze.q: Both the capsule and the stroke look like a bar with rounded ends. Which information in the window would tell them apart, and which would not?
A primitive mesh has 2V minus F equal to 6. List two geometric reasons that could produce it.
analyze.hint: Use 2V - F = 2 chi + B, where B counts boundary edges.

evaluate.q: Is a screenshot with no printed parameters adequate evidence that a primitive is correct? What would you add?
evaluate.hint: A printed radius, a volume and a comparison against the formula.

evaluate.q: The mesh is a sampled approximation. For which of these shapes would a coarse resolution hide the most error, and why?
evaluate.hint: Think of curvature: where do flat triangles depart most from the surface.

create: Design a one-line caption template for primitive screenshots that always states the node, parameters, resolution, scale and closed-surface check.
Write a test that builds each primitive at three resolutions and verifies that the volume converges to the exact formula.

checks.q: What does a negative value of the signed distance mean?
checks.hint: Which side of the surface is the point on?
checks.answer: The point is inside the body. Zero means on the surface and positive means outside.

checks.q: A closed mesh has 3000 vertices. How many triangles does it have if it is ball-like?
A mesh has V = 6432 and F = 12856. What is chi and what could the surface be?
checks.answer: 2V - F = 8 so chi = 4. Two ball-like closed surfaces fit, for example a solid with an internal cavity.

checks.q: Two primitive screenshots show the same disc outline, but one scale bar says 200 micrometres and the other says 2 mm. Are the bodies the same size?
checks.answer: No. The outline is the same in pixels, but the scale bar says the second body is ten times larger. Always read the bar.

checks.q: How would you test a torus implementation with the information in a screenshot like this?
checks.hint: Combine the counts with a known volume.
checks.answer: Check that chi is 0 from V and F, then compute the volume from the mesh and compare it with 2 pi squared R r squared at several resolutions; the error should fall as the resolution rises.
